newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel may slow settlement to save talks - report.
newsitem.headline: Israel may slow settlement to save talks - report.

text.p: Israel and the PLO may break their talks impasse with a compromise accord under which the Jewish state would go on building a disputed settlement, but at a "slow pace close to stoppage", a newspaper said on Monday.
Prodded by Egyptian mediation, Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met formally for the first time in more than two months on Sunday in Cairo.

The talks were plunged into crisis in March, when Israel enraged the PLO by sending bulldozers to break ground for a new settlement on an East Jerusalem hilltop which Israelis call Har Homa and Palestinians refer to as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
The sides ..."now are leaning toward solving the Har Homa issue with Israel agreeing to keep building at a 'slow pace close to stoppage'", the Israeli daily Haaretz reported.

The paper, quoting diplomatic sources, said the compromise ..."allows Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to show Israel has not stopped work at the site, at the same time the Palestinians can say the (settlement) activity is equivalent to a freeze".

Netanyahu, pressed by hawkish coalition partners who threaten to topple his slim six-vote majority in the 120-seat parliament, has declared he will resist Palestinian demands he curb settlement work as a condition for progress in the talks.
His spokesman Shai Bazak, declining to discuss the details of the Haaretz report, said "work is proceeding at a regular pace" at the settlement. He did not elaborate.
Palestinians say the Israeli home building at Jabel Abu Ghneim pre-empts discussions on the final status of Jerusalem, one of a series of core issues the sides have pledged to settle by 1999.
Israel's Channel One television said on Sunday Netanyahu might be considering a clandestine end to Har Homa settlement.
Israeli right-wingers served notice that a halt to settlement work would spell the end of his government.
Jerusalem Mayor Ehud Olmert, a member of Netanyahu's hardline Likud party, said of a possible settlement freeze: "You cannot do these things secretly.
"I do not think there is anyone who deludes himself that we can fool ourselves into thinking that we have not stopped when in fact we have," Olmert told Channel Two television on Monday.

Israel claimed East Jerusalem as part of its capital after capturing it in the 1967 Middle East war. The claim is unrecognised internationally. The PLO sees East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

A senior Palestinian official said on Monday the talks with Israel could resume on Thursday. The official, Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, secretary-general of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's office, expressed surprise at comments by Egyptian and Israeli officials that progress had been made on Sunday.
"But in any case, it seems that there will be another meeting next Thursday and it will be a three-way meeting," Abdel-Rahim told Israeli Arabic radio.
Michael Stoltz, a spokesman for Netanyahu, said no meeting had been scheduled yet, "but I wouldn't rule one out".

Egyptian mediator Osama el-Baz said after more than three hours of peace talks in Cairo on Sunday: "It was a very good meeting held in a very positive atmosphere and some progress was made but we need more talks in order to bridge the gaps."
Baz, who has recently shuttled between the Palestinians and Israelis, declined to say if settlements had been discussed.

Egypt, which considers itself an unofficial sponsor of the peace talks, has intensified its role in the peace crisis since a summit between Mubarak and Netanyahu last month. Analysts say it has even replaced the United States as the main mediator.

Diplomatic sources say Egypt is pushing a five-point plan which included a freeze on any change in the status of Jerusalem and a ban on Jewish settlement building in the West Bank for "a sufficient period". In return the Palestinians would give a firm commitment to address Israel's security demands.
